t: Max Value of Equation — Monotonic Deque Editorial
o:
We must pick two points i < j (so xj > xi) with xj - xi <= k maximizing yi + yj + (xj - xi). Since points are sorted by x, |xi - xj| = xj - xi, so the value equals (yj + xj) + (yi - xi): a fixed part for j plus a quantity depending only on i. For each j we want the maximum of yi - xi among earlier points with xi >= xj - k. Constraints allow n up to 1e5, so O(n^2) brute force is too slow; a sliding-window structure over the sorted x's gives O(n).

Example 1: for j = [2,0], only point [1,3] is in window; value 0+2+3-1=4. For j=[6,-10], window covers [5,10] and [6,-10]; best is 10-5=5, giving -10+6+5=1. Max is 4.

Example 2: for j=[3,0], window is [0,0]; value 0+3+0-0=3.
k: Rewrite yi + yj + |xi - xj| as (yi - xi) + (yj + xj) since xj > xi, splitting the equation into a per-j constant and a per-i term.
For each j, the valid predecessors form a contiguous suffix of points with x in [xj - k, xj), so a sliding window works.
A monotonic deque keeping indices with decreasing yi - xi gives O(1) amortized max queries.

a.i: Try every pair (i, j) with i < j, check xj - xi <= k, and track the maximum of yi + yj + (xj - xi). This directly mirrors the problem statement and is fine to mention first, but with n up to 1e5 it is too slow in the worst case.
s: For each j from 1 to n-1, for each i from 0 to j-1:
If points[j][0] - points[i][0] <= k, update ans with yi + yj + (xj - xi); otherwise break inner loop early since x's are sorted.
a.t: O(n^2) worst case — all pairs may satisfy the constraint; the break helps when windows are small but doesn't bound worst case.

a.i: Sweep j left to right maintaining a max-heap of (yi - xi, xi) pairs. Before processing j, pop entries whose x is more than k behind xj (they can never be valid again since x only increases). Then the heap top is the best predecessor; combine and push (yj - xj, xj).
s: Create a max-heap ordered by yi - xi (store (yi - xi, xi)).
For each point j in order: pop heap tops with xj - top.x > k.
If heap non-empty, candidate = (yj + xj) + top value; update answer.
Push (yj - xj, xj) onto the heap.
a.t: O(n log n) — each point is pushed and popped at most once, with log n heap operations.

a.i: The same sliding window as the heap approach, but a deque storing indices with strictly decreasing yi - xi values answers the window-max query in O(1) amortized. Front holds the current best; expired front elements are popped from the left; new elements pop smaller-or-equal back elements from the right before being appended.
s: Maintain a deque of indices whose yi - xi values are decreasing from front to back.
For each j: pop from the front while xj - x(front) > k.
If deque non-empty, update ans with (yj + xj) + (y(front) - x(front)).
Pop from the back while y(back) - x(back) <= yj - xj, then push j.
a.t: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the deque at most once, so total deque operations are linear.
a.sp: O(n) for the deque in the worst case.

w: In an interview, start by deriving the algebraic split (yi - xi) + (yj + xj) — that reframing is the whole problem. Then present the sliding-window observation and implement the monotonic deque for O(n); the heap version is an acceptable fallback if you're less comfortable with deques. Pitfalls: forgetting that |xi - xj| = xj - xi only because x's are strictly increasing; using 32-bit arithmetic carelessly (values reach ~4e8, safe in int, but intermediate sums in C++/Java should use long to be safe); popping equal values from the back is optional but keeps the deque smaller. Edge cases: k = 0 (only pairs with identical x, impossible here since x strictly increases — but the guarantee ensures some pair exists, so trust the input), negative coordinates, and n = 2. Follow-ups: what if points weren't sorted (sort first, O(n log n)); what if you needed the actual pair of indices (track argmax alongside the deque front).
